title: Capstone: a prediction project from start to finish
summary: Load a CSV with pandas, clean it, split it, beat a baseline and report honest held-out accuracy.

sources.section: Chapter 14: Working with CSV Files and JSON Data

license: Original work for Python Intelligence; license to be chosen by the owner
objective: Run a whole learning pipeline: clean the data, avoid leakage, compare against a baseline and report honestly.
analogy: A pipeline is a kitchen line: clean ingredients first, keep the tasting spoon (the test set) out of the cooking, and always compare with the plain dish (the baseline).

misconceptions.belief: A model is good if its accuracy is high.
misconceptions.correction: Compare with a baseline such as predicting the majority class; 90% may be no better.

misconceptions.belief: Cleaning or scaling the whole dataset before splitting is harmless.
misconceptions.correction: Statistics from the test rows leak into training; fit cleaning steps on training data.

misconceptions.belief: A feature that predicts the target perfectly is a great find.
misconceptions.correction: It is often leakage, information that wouldn't exist at prediction time.

rubric.evidence: missing and duplicate rows are handled as specified
the model is compared with a simple baseline
features copied from the target and test-set statistics are kept out

review.recall: Why compare a model with a baseline? Give one example of data leakage.

steps.title: Putting the pieces together
steps.body:
You can now load tables, measure data, split it fairly and train two kinds of classifier. A real
project uses all of them in one order: **load** the raw data, **clean** it, **split** it, set a
**baseline**, **train** on the training part only, then **evaluate** on the held-out part. Each step
is small. The project goes wrong when a step is skipped or done in the wrong order.

steps.title: Two habits that keep the result honest
steps.body:
First, always compare against a **baseline**: the score of a model that does something trivial, such
as always guessing the most common class. If your model can't beat that, it hasn't learned anything
useful, whatever its accuracy looks like. Second, treat the test set as sealed: everything the model
learns, including the class averages and even the baseline's guess, comes from the training data.
Using the test rows while training is called **data leakage**, and it makes results look better than
they will be on new data.

questions: Why might a model that scores 70% be worse than useless?
If you fill missing values with the average of the whole table, test rows included, which habit have you broken?

steps.title: Watch the baseline pick its guess
steps.body: The majority baseline counts the training labels and guesses the most common one. Each frame shows the variables just before the highlighted line runs; the last frame shows what that line printed.

frames.note: Find the most common training label.
First time we see 'palm': get() returns the default 0.
max() looks at the labels in sorted order, so a tie would go to the label that sorts first.

steps.title: The precise rules
steps.body:
**Load:** a CSV file is plain text in which each line is usually one row, with values separated by
commas. In this lesson's files the first line holds the column names (a header, which CSV files may
or may not have; quoted fields can even contain commas or line breaks). `pd.read_csv` reads CSV into
a DataFrame, from a file path or any file-like object, so `io.StringIO(text)` lets it read a string.

**Clean:** `df.isna()` marks missing values. `df.dropna(subset=columns)` drops only the rows that
are missing one of the columns you will use, so a gap in an unused column costs you nothing. Select
the feature columns with `df[columns]`.

**Split:** shuffle the row positions with a seeded `random.Random(seed).shuffle`, then hold out the
first `int(n × test_fraction)` positions as the test set (the recipe from the evaluation lesson).

**Baseline** (the simple reference model this lesson uses): the majority baseline always predicts the
most common training label. `value_counts()` shows the counts.

**Train and evaluate:** fit the model on the training rows only, then report accuracy on the test
rows, next to the baseline's accuracy on the same rows. This is an estimate of how the model will do
on data it has never seen.

steps.title: Run it: inspect the raw data
steps.body: A small survey of plants. Before predicting how many rows survive cleaning, look at which values are missing.
steps.code:
import io
import pandas as pd

PLANTS = 'height,leaf,site,species
12.0,3.1,north,fern
14.5,2.8,,fern
30.2,7.5,south,palm
11.1,,north,fern
28.4,8.1,south,palm
13.3,3.6,east,fern
26.0,6.2,east,palm
16.8,4.4,north,fern
22.5,5.9,south,palm
19.0,5.0,east,fern
24.1,4.6,,palm
9.5,2.2,east,moss
10.4,2.6,north,moss
'

df = pd.read_csv(io.StringIO(PLANTS))
print(df.shape)
print(df.isna().sum().to_dict())

clean = df.dropna(subset=['height', 'leaf', 'species'])
print(clean.shape)
print(clean['species'].value_counts().sort_index().to_dict())

steps.title: Your turn: from CSV text to examples
steps.body:
Complete `load_examples(csv_text, features, label)`. Read the CSV with pandas, drop the rows missing
any of the `features` columns or the `label` column (keep rows that are only missing other
columns), and return `(X, y)`: `X` is a list with one list of floats per row, in the order the
`features` are given, and `y` is the list of labels.
hints: `df.dropna(subset=features + [label])` drops only the rows with a gap in those columns.
`df[features].astype(float).values.tolist()` turns the selected columns into a list of lists of floats.

steps.title: Challenge: the whole pipeline
steps.body:
The starter gives you `load_examples`, `fit_centroids` and `predict_centroids`. Write
`run_pipeline(csv_text, features, label, test_fraction, seed)`:

1. Load and clean the examples with `load_examples`.
2. Shuffle the positions `0 … n−1` of the cleaned rows with `random.Random(seed).shuffle`; the first
   `int(n * test_fraction)` positions are the test set and the rest the training set. Raise
   `ValueError` if either set is empty.
3. The baseline guess is the most common **training** label (a tie goes to the label first in sorted
   order; labels may be text or numbers, and numbers sort as numbers).
4. Fit the centroids on the **training** rows only with `fit_centroids`, and predict the test rows with
   `predict_centroids`.

Return a dictionary with `'n_train'`, `'n_test'`, `'baseline_label'`, and the test-set accuracies
`'baseline'` and `'model'`, as unrounded floats.
hints: Write two small helpers first: `majority_label(labels)` (the trace above) and `accuracy(predicted, actual)`.
Build the four lists `X_train`, `y_train`, `X_test`, `y_test` from the shuffled positions, and never pass a test row to `fit_centroids` or `majority_label`.

tests.name: the model sees exactly the training rows
tests.code:
PLANTS = 'height,leaf,site,species\n12.0,3.1,north,fern\n14.5,2.8,,fern\n30.2,7.5,south,palm\n11.1,,north,fern\n28.4,8.1,south,palm\n13.3,3.6,east,fern\n26.0,6.2,east,palm\n16.8,4.4,north,fern\n22.5,5.9,south,palm\n19.0,5.0,east,fern\n24.1,4.6,,palm\n9.5,2.2,east,moss\n10.4,2.6,north,moss\n'
X = [[12.0, 3.1], [14.5, 2.8], [30.2, 7.5], [28.4, 8.1], [13.3, 3.6], [26.0, 6.2], [16.8, 4.4], [22.5, 5.9], [19.0, 5.0], [24.1, 4.6], [9.5, 2.2], [10.4, 2.6]]
y = ['fern', 'fern', 'palm', 'palm', 'fern', 'palm', 'fern', 'palm', 'fern', 'palm', 'moss', 'moss']
pos = list(range(12))
random.Random(33).shuffle(pos)
want_fit = sorted((tuple(X[i]), y[i]) for i in pos[4:])
want_pred = sorted(tuple(X[i]) for i in pos[:4])
seen = {}
_fit, _pred = fit_centroids, predict_centroids

def fit_centroids(X, y):
    seen['fit'] = sorted((tuple(float(v) for v in r), l) for r, l in zip(X, y))
    return _fit(X, y)

def predict_centroids(c, X):
    seen['pred'] = sorted(tuple(float(v) for v in r) for r in X)
    return _pred(c, X)

try:
    run_pipeline(PLANTS, ['height', 'leaf'], 'species', 0.4, 33)
finally:
    fit_centroids, predict_centroids = _fit, _pred
assert seen.get('fit') == want_fit, 'call fit_centroids once with exactly the 8 training rows: no test row, none missing'
assert seen.get('pred') == want_pred, 'call predict_centroids with exactly the 4 test rows'

steps.title: Transfer: a pipeline audit
steps.body:
Write `clean(df)`: return a new DataFrame without rows that have any missing value and without duplicate rows (keep the
first), with a fresh 0..n−1 index. Write `majority_baseline(y_train, y_test)`: the accuracy on `y_test` of always
predicting the most common label in `y_train` (ties to the smallest label). Write `leaky_columns(df, target)`: the
sorted names of other columns whose values equal the target column in every row.
hints: Count labels with `value_counts()`; for leakage, compare each column with `df[c].equals(df[target])`.

tests.name: drops missing and duplicate rows
tests.code:
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
df = pd.DataFrame({'a': [1, 1, 2, np.nan], 'b': ['x', 'x', 'y', 'z']})
out = clean(df)
assert out.to_dict('list') == {'a': [1.0, 2.0], 'b': ['x', 'y']} and list(out.index) == [0, 1], out
assert len(df) == 4, 'return a new DataFrame'

tests.name: the majority baseline
tests.code: assert majority_baseline([1, 0, 1, 1], [1, 0, 0, 1]) == 0.5 and majority_baseline([0, 1], [0, 0, 1]) == 2 / 3

tests.name: columns that copy the target
tests.code:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({'y': [0, 1, 1], 'copy': [0, 1, 1], 'z': [0, 1, 0], 'also': [0, 1, 1]})
assert leaky_columns(df, 'y') == ['also', 'copy'], leaky_columns(df, 'y')

tests.name: the steps fit together
tests.code:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({'f': [1, 2, 2, None], 'label': [1, 0, 0, 1]})
c = clean(df)
assert majority_baseline(c['label'], c['label']) == 0.5 and leaky_columns(c, 'label') == []

questions.prompt: Your model scores 0.72 on the test set. The majority baseline scores 0.80 on the same rows. What does that tell you?
choices: The model is worse than always guessing the most common class
The model is good: 0.72 is high
The test set is too small to say anything
questions.explanation: A model only earns its keep by beating the trivial baseline on the same data.

questions.prompt: Which of these is data leakage?
choices: Computing the class centroids from all the rows, then testing on some of them
questions.explanation: The test rows influenced the model, so the test score is no longer an honest estimate.

questions.prompt: A CSV has 50 rows. 4 are missing a feature you use and 3 others are missing only a column you don't use. How many rows does `dropna(subset=...)` keep with your columns?
questions.explanation: Only the 4 rows missing a used column are dropped.

questions.prompt: Why fix the seed when splitting?
choices: So the same split, and the same reported score, can be reproduced
So the test set is always the last rows
questions.explanation: With a fixed seed anyone can rerun the pipeline and get identical numbers.

steps.title: What you can do now
steps.body:
